title: Michelangelo carved David from a marble block two sculptors had given up on

cover.alt: Michelangelo’s marble David in the Galleria dell’Accademia, Florence: the nude figure stands with his weight on one leg, sling over his shoulder, beneath a domed skylight.

body: The block of Carrara marble that became David was bought in 1465 for the sculptor Agostino di Duccio, who roughed out a torso and legs and then stopped. Antonio Rossellino was hired to continue in 1476, but his contract was apparently rescinded, and the block, nicknamed *il gigante*, lay neglected for about 25 more years. In 1501 the 26-year-old Michelangelo won the commission and began carving on 13 September; the finished **5.17 m** figure was unveiled on 8 September 1504. It had been meant for a buttress high on the cathedral, but raising it there was judged all but impossible, so it stood beside the Palazzo della Signoria instead.

slides.alt: A 19th-century photograph of Michelangelo’s David standing outdoors on its pedestal in the Piazza della Signoria, with the palace wall behind it.
slides.caption: David outdoors in the Piazza della Signoria, photographed around 1860–70, shortly before it moved indoors to the Accademia in 1873.

slides.question: How tall is the statue, in centimetres?
slides.explanation: 5.17 m of marble, so tall that workers had nicknamed the block ‘the giant’ decades before Michelangelo touched it.

slides.heading: A block that waited 36 years
slides.note: Agostino di Duccio had the contract from 1464 and acquired the block the next year.

slides.heading: Stones, a riot and a hammer
slides.text: Protesters pelted the statue with stones in its first year. In 1527 an anti-Medici riot broke its left arm into three pieces. In 1991 a man attacked it with a hidden hammer and broke off the tip of a toe on the left foot. Nearly 1.5 million people a year now come to see it, about 4,000 a day when the gallery is open.

slides.question: Where was David originally meant to stand?
slides.explanation: It was commissioned as one of twelve prophets for the buttresses of Florence Cathedral, but hoisting a 5 m marble that high was judged scarcely possible.

slides.heading: Cracks in the ankles
slides.text: Monitoring shows the statue leaning forward by 1 to 3 degrees, which has played a major part in hairline cracks at the ankles, though engineering analyses find it stable. One study traces the tilt to a flood in 1844. The spots most watched now are the tree-stump support behind the right leg and the left ankle and heel.
